body.text: The retreat of traditional donors is an opening for India in its neighbourhood, but only if it delivers faster, publishes more, and reorganises how it structures its aid
Image Source: Getty Images

Buried in the annual report of Suriname's national audit office is a grateful acknowledgement of continued Indian technical assistance that has helped Suriname over the years. Officers have been sent to India for training under the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) programme; on returning, the office began running its own courses for Suriname's civil service on procurement rules, financial statements, and bank reconciliation.

This is just one instance of where India's comparative advantage as a development partner lies. As traditional donors retreat, the instinctive question is whether India can replace the volume being withdrawn. It probably cannot - and more importantly, it should not spend precious resources trying to do that. What India can do is scale what it already does cheaply and well: training, standards, digital public infrastructure (DPI), and institutional capacity. The case for making these the centrepiece of Indian development policy has never been stronger.

The decline in aid volume currently underway is not normal or cyclical. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) June 2026 assessment, net Official Development Assistance (ODA) fell by 23.3 percent in 2025 — the largest single-year drop ever recorded — following a reduction of 8.5 percent in 2024 and is projected to fall a further 6.9 percent in 2026.

For the first time in nearly three decades, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States all cut ODA in the same year: 2024. Given 2025 events, it also marks the first time in the history of the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) that all four have cut aid simultaneously for two years running. Beyond those four, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Switzerland have announced reductions of their own.

According to McKinsey's analysis of announced reductions, projected cuts vary widely by sector — anywhere from 2 to 37 percent of the 2023 baseline. Early evidence from terminated US contracts suggests education, energy, and administrative spending are being cut hardest. Sub-sectors funded by a concentration of few donors are structurally fragile: only two donors alone account for more than half of ODA for relief coordination and emergency food assistance. Sectors that rely heavily on multilateral channels — water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); agriculture and food; health, each drawing at least 30 percent of their ODA multilaterally — are exposed twice over, once to bilateral cuts and again to the pass-through effect on multilateral budgets.

The good news is that India is already the dominant alternative provider in South Asia. It committed INR 10,000 crore to Bhutan's 13th Five-Year Plan, supplied roughly 72 percent of all international grant aid received by the Maldives in 2025, and extended over US$4 billion in emergency assistance to Sri Lanka after the 2022 crisis. The question is not whether India can enter the aid vacuum left by other donors, but whether it can scale within a region where it already has a dominant position.

Why does this matter for India? According to the OECD, four Least Developed Countries (LDCs) sit in South Asia — Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar — and net bilateral ODA to them is expected to fall by between 1 percent and 8 percent from 2023 levels. CGD's country-level analysis shows Afghanistan ranking second worldwide for bilateral ODA reductions measured against gross national income, with Sri Lanka and Nepal also heavily exposed to the US withdrawal. It committed INR 10,000 crore to Bhutan's 13th Five-Year Plan, supplied roughly 72 percent of all international grant aid received by the Maldives in 2025, and extended over US$4 billion in emergency assistance to Sri Lanka after the 2022 crisis. The question is not whether India can enter the aid vacuum left by other donors, but whether it can scale within a region where it already has a dominant position.

In Afghanistan, US funding was roughly 108 times India’s; in Bangladesh, roughly 28 times. The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) alone accounted for about 35 percent of all international assistance to Afghanistan. The gap is not one India can close by writing larger aid cheques. India needs to figure out an entry strategy rather than a replacement strategy. Tuberculosis, reproductive health, maternal and child nutrition, and WASH are areas where India has domestic delivery experience, comparatively low unit costs, and a plausible claim to comparative advantage. They are also areas where the withdrawal of donor funding is acute and where targeted action can yield outsized visibility.

Separately, a vulnerability India faces is credibility, not capacity. India’s persistent issue has never really been the size of its allocation; it has been the interval between announcement and delivery. Project cycles run slow, and the gap between what is budgeted and what is disbursed is a structural feature rather than an occasional lapse.

In 2024–25, budgeted assistance across all partner countries came to roughly INR 4,883.56 crore, against a total Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) budget of about INR 22,154 crore. In 2025–26, the development assistance portfolio rose to INR 6,750 crore — a year-on-year increase of about 20 percent, and roughly 33 percent of an MEA allocation of INR 20,516.61 crore. South Asia took 57.65 percent of the total, its highest share since 2018–19. The 2026–27 budget puts the total MEA allocation at INR 22,118.97 crore, with the ‘Aid to Countries’ line at INR 5,685.56 crore. This 2026–27 allocation is slightly lower than the previous year's, which seems to be the result of a cautious turn given recent political developments in Dhaka. Reflecting a broader shift in the nature of development assistance, grant assistance is now subsumed by concessional development finance. The Export Import Bank of India (Exim Bank) holds 258 lines of credit across 64 countries worth around US$25.48 billion, concessional by international standards at a 63 percent average grant element, but requiring 75 percent Indian procurement — combining export promotion and development finance.

The binding constraint, however, is administrative rather than fiscal. The United States, for instance, recruits anywhere between 300 and 900 foreign service officers a year. The Indian Foreign Service fields roughly 954 officers across 194 diplomatic missions. A demand-driven model routing every partner request through a thinly staffed Development Partnership Administration (DPA) cannot meet the growing need for specialised knowledge and targeted delivery. On top of that, the MEA’s training allocation fell by 1.6 percent in 2026–27 even as development ambitions expanded.

India has consistently pressed for transparency in others’ development finance frameworks while maintaining an opaque framework for its overseas engagements. The MEA Dashboard currently publishes only country-level aggregates. Independent analysts must assemble India’s picture from scattered sources, which limits external evaluation and quietly undercuts India’s claim to moral authority in Global South development debates.

A transparency deficit compounds the problem. India has consistently pressed for transparency in others’ development finance frameworks while maintaining an opaque framework for its overseas engagements. The MEA Dashboard currently publishes only country-level aggregates. Independent analysts must assemble India’s picture from scattered sources, which limits external evaluation and quietly undercuts India’s claim to moral authority in Global South development debates.
If the constraint is institutional rather than fiscal, the reform agenda can be deduced fairly directly:

1) Execution over Announcement: A dedicated project implementation tracking framework within the Development Partnership Administration of the MEA, operating against quarterly delivery benchmarks, would address the single most damaging feature of India’s current record. Expanding the IFS to a strength of around 1,500 officers, with lateral recruitment of development finance, infrastructure, and technology specialists and improving inter-ministerial coordination mechanisms would be the next logical step.

2) Specialised Agencies: The deeper problem is that India runs commercial export promotion, strategic infrastructure, and concessional development assistance through overlapping institutions with a single ministry as the coordinating node. A cleaner division could mean giving autonomy to Exim Bank of India as a commercial and export-credit institution, increasing reliance on the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NABFID) along the lines of the United States International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) for strategically motivated investment, using state-owned banks for sectoral priorities, and establishing a dedicated agency for genuine ODA like the Chinese CIDCA (China International Development Cooperation Agency).

3) Engage Recipient Societies: India has faced considerable blowback in recent years for anchoring its aid programmes in neighbourhood regimes rather than in the societal and structural realities of recipient countries. The alternative is institutionalised programmes aimed at civil society, business communities, and young professionals in partner countries, so that Indian investment survives changes of government in Dhaka, Kathmandu, or Malé. The same logic argues for working through local partners and local expertise in delivery — both because projects designed without local context underperform, and because of the documented risk of assistance being captured by recipient-country elites rather than reaching its intended beneficiaries.

4) Publish Annual Development Partnership Reports: An annual development cooperation report, modelled on Japan’s ODA white paper or the United Kingdom’s statistics on international development, would do three things at once: build the internal data infrastructure India currently lacks, allow external evaluation, and remove the most obvious inconsistency in India’s Global South positioning.

5) Leverage Domestic Philanthropic Capital: Given budget constraints, aid volume need not come from the exchequer alone. India's philanthropic capital has expanded substantially, and blended structures pooling public, private, and philanthropic funds are drawing serious attention as traditional aid contracts. Channelling a fraction toward neighbourhood partnerships would widen India's offer without competing directly against domestic capital expenditure.

As traditional ODA declines, the question is what will replace it. In this vacuum, India can deliver faster, publish more, separate its commercial lending from its concessional assistance, and concentrate on targeted instruments — training, digital public infrastructure, health systems, and rapid crisis liquidity.

The retreat of traditional ODA is eroding more than the volume of aid and development cooperation. The reporting standards, evaluation norms, and coordination mechanisms that made DAC assistance auditable are also weakening, just as non-DAC providers are becoming large enough to matter systemically. As traditional ODA declines, the question is what will replace it. In this vacuum, India can deliver faster, publish more, separate its commercial lending from its concessional assistance, and concentrate on targeted instruments — training, digital public infrastructure, health systems, and rapid crisis liquidity.

Ameya Joshi is a Program Manager at AidData, William & Mary, where he works on China’s sovereign lending, its debt restructuring architecture, and its overseas financing of critical mineral extraction and processing.
